name: Bianca Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers stay confidential. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Bianca, 43, with a bachelor’s in music. I lead a small wedding string group, record violin lines for local adverts and teach beginner violin after school. I have played for years and can keep an event moving, though I am a solid working player rather than a star. I love seeing a family dance to a tune their parents knew; I dislike chasing a recording fee after the client has used the track.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that pay fit your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner does seasonal building work, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My music pay is low for the hours, our savings are under a month’s expenses, and there are few similar jobs nearby. I use AI every day for booking messages and practice drafts, but I play every exercise before a pupil sees it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the wedding group that faster messages are welcome, but the couple still wants people who can follow a changing room. I expect our Saturday dates and my pupils to carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our account is thin even if AI mostly disappoints. A late wedding payment and a short building-work week would make us move money between the electricity and mortgage bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the three weekly pupils, the two booked weddings and my small advert recordings this winter. Through the first year I’d put each cleared session fee toward the electricity balance before buying new strings, and check the Saturday deposit dates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household before any big technology change. I can get on with playing. A single cancelled wedding makes the kitchen table feel very quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which ordinary bill makes you check the diary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The electricity bill can wait a week; the mortgage lender is less patient. I would ask for a payment date before booking a sitter for a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you keep away from an AI tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not upload a child’s violin take or a couple’s first dance recording just to speed up a message. I already use AI for drafts, but the families’ sound belongs to them.

say: I would welcome faster **booking messages** while keeping Saturday performances live.
I would tell the wedding group that players still need to **follow the room**.
think: Our **mortgage** already strains against seasonal building pay and a thin account.
A late **wedding deposit** could shift money away from electricity.
do: Keep three **pupils**, two weddings and advert recordings this winter.
Use cleared **session fees** for electricity before new strings and confirm Saturday deposits in writing.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a cancelled wedding already reaches household bills.
S0.quote: A single cancelled wedding makes the kitchen table feel very quiet.
fieldNote: Her **thin savings** and partner’s seasonal pay drive worry even under Plateau.
Daily **AI drafts** help with messages, but she protects family recordings and pupil audio.

steps.text: Keep three pupils, two booked weddings and advert recordings this winter
Delay new strings until cleared session fees cover electricity balance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a cheap generated advert track is a real competitor, and musicians must show why a played line is worth buying. I would quote live playing separately from a file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advert recordings cover school shoes and fuel. If those orders shrink, I can still play weddings, but winter Saturdays are not enough to make the mortgage painless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI score-checking tool on lines I own, comparing its notes with my violin before using it for paid work. In the first year, if advert orders fall, I’d run a paid family fiddle hour at the independent church hall only if the hall provides space, six families prepay enough for my time and my partner can cover pickup; I’d stop renting my separate recording booth on empty weekdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the lost fees would reach home quickly, though I can test a class. I will not spend the mortgage money on a room full of people who only said they might come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which paid recording would disappear first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A thirty-second advert line is small on paper, but two of those fees buy school shoes and a week of fuel. I would list cancelled orders before paying for more studio time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a new workshop worth the family time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hour needs six paid families, a room without a deposit and a pickup plan for our children. If only five pay, I would refund them rather than turn a family evening into debt.

say: I would price **live violin** separately from a generated advert file.
I would tell clients a played line must **earn its fee**.
think: Advert **recordings** help pay for the children’s school shoes and fuel.
Winter **weddings** cannot reliably replace lost weekday fees through the quiet months.
do: Learn new **AI score checking** on owned lines this month, checking notes on violin before paid use.
Run paid **fiddle hour** in first year if adverts fall, hall space is free, six families prepay and pickup is covered.
Stop renting the **recording booth** on empty weekdays if advert orders fall.
feel: I feel **anxious** about advert fees reaching household money quickly.
S1.quote: I will not spend the mortgage money on a room full of people who only said they might come.
fieldNote: She distinguishes daily **AI drafts** from genuinely new score checking tested on her own violin lines.
The **fiddle hour** needs free space, six prepayments for teaching and confirmed child pickup.

steps.text: Learn score checker on owned lines; compare with violin before using for paid work
Run fiddle hour first year if adverts fall, room free, six prepay and pickup covered
Stop renting booth on empty weekdays if advert orders fall in first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell wedding clients that thinking AGI by 2028 could make scores and advert lines cheaply, while robots able to play hands-on parts follow around 2031. I would not call those three years a guarantee of bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert orders could stop in 2028, and some parents may buy app lessons. My partner’s building pay is seasonal, so losing both my weekday streams could make the mortgage hard within weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d ask each wedding client for written dates and count what the advert work pays. In the first year after AGI arrives, if advert orders stop, I’d cancel the recording booth at renewal, ask the lender about a temporary plan before missing a mortgage payment, and apply for a posted music-shop sales job only if I meet its requirements and written net pay covers travel and school pickup; I’d keep pupils until a real offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed. A year of weddings looks busy on a calendar, but it is not money in the account until deposits clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens before a robot could play your violin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The recorded violin line can be copied before a robot ever holds a bow. Even if Saturday work lasts to 2031, there are long weekdays between weddings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask family to pay the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my parents to watch the children for a job interview only if they are free, not ask them to cover our mortgage. I would confirm a pickup before promising a shop my afternoon.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from robot violinists around 2031.
I would tell clients that **live bookings** still need deposits, not guesses.
think: Advert orders and some **pupil lessons** may vanish quickly.
Seasonal **building pay** cannot cover the mortgage without my weekday fees.
do: Keep **current pupils** until a real shop offer; confirm wedding dates and advert income before 2028.
Cancel **recording booth** at renewal in first year after 2028 if orders stop.
Ask **lender** before arrears and seek qualifying posted shop work if adverts stop; require written net pay covering travel/pickup.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because two weekday streams could vanish with almost no savings.
S2.quote: The recorded violin line can be copied before a robot ever holds a bow.
fieldNote: Thinking AI could remove **2028 advert work** before physical robot players arrive around 2031.
A shop application needs a **real vacancy**, qualification and written net pay after travel and pickup.

steps.text: Keep current pupils until real shop offer; confirm wedding dates and advert income before 2028
Cancel booth at renewal in first year after 2028 if advert orders stop
Ask lender before missed mortgage payment if advert orders stop after 2028
Seek qualifying posted shop role if adverts stop after 2028; written net pay covers travel/pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough to build a paid teaching circle, if families really want one. Thinking AGI in 2031 arrives before capable robot violinists around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have a more regular class by then, but I cannot turn interest into wages. A borrowed room and six real payments matter more than a clever poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I’d ask the independent church hall for one room without a deposit and invite six families to prepay for a four-week fiddle circle. I’d teach it only if those fees cover my time and confirmed childcare; in the first year after 2031 I’d repeat it only while six families pay and the room stays free, keeping the weddings that still book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because our savings are thin now, though five years gives the circle time to prove itself. The mortgage still arrives between school terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build during the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a local player to help for a paid hour only if registrations cover that fee too. An apprentice can watch my bowing at a wedding, but I will not call unpaid work a favour to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the church hall cannot give you space?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the hall cannot provide space without a deposit, I would keep private lessons and wait for another room. I would not put a hall booking on a credit card while our electricity balance is open.

say: I would tell families **2031 thinking AGI** precedes robot violinists around 2034.
I would insist a **paid circle** needs real registrations.
think: A regular **fiddle circle** could replace advert fees only if families prepay.
I cannot use **mortgage money** for a hall deposit.
do: Ask independent hall for **free room** next term and invite six prepayments.
Teach **four-week circle** only if fees cover my time and childcare; add a helper only with their fee covered.
Repeat circle in **first year after 2031** only while six pay and room stays free; keep paid weddings.
feel: I feel **anxious** because present bills continue while the circle is tested.
S3.quote: A borrowed room and six real payments matter more than a clever poster.
fieldNote: She uses **prepayments** and free space to prevent a trial class from draining the mortgage account.
Any **helper** joins only if registration covers their paid hour as well.

steps.text: Start four-week circle only with free room, six prepayments covering teaching and confirmed childcare
Repeat circle first post-2031 year only while six families pay and room stays free
Keep paid weddings while bookings continue
Pay local helper only if registrations also cover their fee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell young players to learn to listen, show up and charge for the work they do. Thinking AGI in 2036 and robot violinists around 2039 give us time, not a reason to give music away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might still lead weddings, or I might teach more children than I play for. Our mortgage and seasonal building pay will still need cash long before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep the three pupils and booked weddings, use cleared advert fees to pay the electricity balance, then save a little when possible. Across the decade I’d run the fiddle circle only with free space, six prepayments covering my time and confirmed pickup; in the first year after 2036 I’d keep paid circles and live dates while they book, and seek a posted school music-room role only if I meet its requirements and net pay covers travel and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the money we have today even with ten years to plan. A longer warning lets me grow a class carefully, but it does not fill the grocery cupboard this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a young apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach an apprentice to read the room, not only the score. I would bring one onto a paid date only if the client’s fee covers their share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you avoid spending your last cushion on a forecast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pay the electricity balance first, then save the next extra session fee after the mortgage and food clear. A forecast is not a reason to borrow for new gear.

I would keep **2036 thinking AGI** separate from robot violinists around 2039.
think: At **53**, I might still lead weddings or teach more pupils.
Our **mortgage** and seasonal building pay require cash long before 2039.
do: Keep **pupils and weddings** this year, clearing electricity arrears before saving.
Run **fiddle circle** through first post-2036 year only with free room, six prepayments and covered pickup.
Seek posted **school work** first post-2036 year only if qualified and net pay covers travel and childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about today’s money even with ten years to prepare.
S4.quote: A forecast is not a reason to borrow for new gear.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** persists because little is saved and building work is seasonal.

Clear electricity arrears then save next extra fee after mortgage and food

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because advert fees and some lessons could stop before the wedding calendar fills. Written deposits, a lender plan priced in full and a real shop vacancy at a net wage that covers pickup would help. I will not ask my parents to pay the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the child watching a parent practise after work. My children hear violin scales every night, but I want them to see a fee next to the music too.

headlineQuote: My children hear violin scales every night, but I want them to see a fee next to the music too.
portrait: Bianca is a **43-year-old violinist** with a music bachelor’s, leading weddings, recording adverts and teaching beginners.
Her **low pay**, seasonal building income, two children and mortgage leave less than one month saved.
She uses **AI daily**, but tests a new score checker on owned lines and guards family recordings.
Fast AGI threatens **advert fees** before robot violinists arrive, so she tests prepaid classes without borrowing.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could remove advert fees and lessons before paid weddings replace them.
whatWouldHelp: Written **wedding deposits** and a fully costed lender plan would buy time.
A real **shop vacancy** with net pay covering pickup would offer replacement work.
